abstract: |
  The Climate Policy Assessment Tool (CPAT) tells a finance ministry what a carbon price raises and what it cuts, but ministries keep asking questions its core cannot answer. What is a mix of standards, subsidies and feebates worth as a carbon price? What will the EU carbon border adjustment cost our exporters? What will the clean capital cost, and should the budget pay for it? How do we link CPAT to the other models we use? What does a climate program do to growth and debt? This section answers each with one upgrade that bolts onto the rebuilt model without changing its core: the Total Effective Carbon Price, the CBAM Policy Tool, a public investment extension, a common activity layer, and the Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool. Each takes CPAT's prices, fuel use and emissions as given, adds one piece of economics, and states its method in a few equations so that a ministry can check it.

*Overview of section 6, version 0.1, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. Companion to the CPAT-AI repository, https://github.com/cpmodelai/cpat_ai, and the Climate Fiscal AI Tools. Country results quoted here are illustrative tool results, not official estimates.*

# A small core and modular upgrades beat one large model {.unnumbered}

A model a ministry can audit has to stay small, and the questions ministries ask keep growing. Section 5 states CPAT's mitigation module in about eighteen equations, rebuilds it twice and checks it against data and other models. That work only pays off if the core stays legible. Every new question answered by adding cells to the core makes the next audit harder.

The papers in this section therefore add capability as separate modules. Each upgrade reads CPAT's outputs (prices, fuel use, power investment, emissions and revenue), adds one piece of economics, and returns a result a ministry can trace back to the core. Each states its method in a few equations, says what it assumes, and labels its country numbers as illustrative. A ministry can adopt one upgrade without the others.

# Measure any policy mix as one carbon price (paper 6.1) {.unnumbered}

Countries cut emissions with taxes, subsidies, standards and mandates, but the standard metrics add up only explicit prices per tonne. They score a fuel standard or a revenue-neutral feebate at zero and count a dollar on coal the same as a dollar on gasoline. The Total Effective Carbon Price is the uniform economy-wide carbon tax that would cut emissions by as much as a given policy mix. It builds on the IMF's carbon-price equivalent.

A nested constant-elasticity model of energy demand gives closed-form abatement weights that split any instrument's effect into fuel switching and demand reduction. The paper gives exact and second-order versions, extends the metric to tradable and non-tradable standards and mandates, and carries elasticity uncertainty through to a range. In a stylized three-sector economy, a mix that explicit-price metrics rate at \$21 per tonne has an effective price of \$37 in the long run (\$32–38 across calibrations) and \$28 after one year.

The metric is the common scale for the rest of the program. It lets crediting schemes pay for policies rather than projects, lets border mechanisms recognize implicit and non-price carbon pricing, and shows governments where their policy mix is weak. The carbon-pricing papers of section 1 use it for policy crediting and border recognition.

# Measure exposure to the EU carbon border adjustment (paper 6.2) {.unnumbered}

Since January 2026, EU importers of steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, hydrogen and electricity have owed a charge on the emissions embedded in what they buy. For many middle-income exporters the charge is large, it rises every year to 2034, and it depends on choices their own governments control: whether producers file verified emissions data and whether the country prices carbon at home.

The CBAM Policy Tool computes the exposure product by product and year by year, and shows how emissions data, a domestic carbon price and rebates change it. Its method fits in five equations. In the public-data example for Turkish hot-rolled steel at €80 per tonne of carbon dioxide, the charge on goods declared at the default value rises from about €107 per tonne in 2026 to €252 at full phase-in, close to half the export price. The tool's application to Egypt shows where emissions data matter most. Egypt has no EU country default for steel, so its gas-based steel would be charged as if it came from the most intensive exporters, and verified data would cut the full-phase-in charge on seven Egyptian exports from about €595 million to €177 million a year.

# Price the clean capital and test whether the budget should pay (paper 6.3) {.unnumbered}

Carbon pricing models say what a policy raises and what it cuts, but not what the clean capital it calls for will cost or whether the budget should pay for it. The public investment extension does both. It turns the physical change CPAT computes into investment needs by country and sector, and prices that capital at the market cost of capital, at a social rate, and at a social rate with co-benefits counted.

The cost of capital decides the answer. For a stylized asset whose fuel savings are 13.3 cents a year per dollar of capital, the financial case fails above a cost of capital of 12.6 percent, almost exactly the rate CPAT already assumes for lower-middle-income countries. That links this upgrade to the de-risking papers of section 3. A second test asks what each dollar of net public money buys, against the cost of raising tax, with haircuts for delivery and capital, operating and contract routes on one footing. In a stylized island case, a \$108 million solar plant fails the budget on a seven-year loan; a concessional loan or a guaranteed power purchase agreement rescues it. Country runs put 2030 investment needs in Kenya, Uganda and St Lucia at 4 to 5 percent of GDP, and a SISEPUEDE run for Uganda shows that under a fifth of its net-zero benefits reach the budget as cash.

# Give linked models one activity layer (paper 6.4) {.unnumbered}

Every energy and emissions model starts from activity levels, and the models used in climate-fiscal work build them in incompatible ways. CPAT grows fuel use with GDP and prices. SISEPUEDE grows physical activity with income and population but never with prices. The CBAM tool grows output of steel, aluminum, fertilizer and clinker with growth forecasts and a price response. The Future Technology Transformations models take demand as given.

The activity layer maps each model's activity onto ten common activities and drives all of them with one constant-elasticity rule in population, income per person and the cost of the energy service. The models can then be linked without counting a price response twice. Under stylized growth of 1 percent a year in population and 2 percent in income per person, cars in use grow 64 percent in ten years while travel grows 41 percent.

# Link energy investment to growth, revenue and debt (paper 6.5) {.unnumbered}

A ministry weighing a climate investment program needs its budget cost, what carbon pricing could pay for, and what both do to growth and debt, usually from separate teams. The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool chains them in one workbook for 186 countries. It combines a model of mitigation investment needs split by who pays; a screen for the most abatement a carbon tax, a feebate or a mix can deliver within limits on political cost; simplified, open versions of three IMF and World Bank macro-fiscal models; and a debt sustainability test.

Financing matters more than size. In a stylized run, how the program is financed and how efficiently public investment is spent move the result more than the size of the program. A run for Kenya finds a net zero budget need of 0.5 percent of GDP in 2030, mostly land-use and non-CO₂ spending rather than capital. Feasible power-sector carbon pricing covers about 5 percent of it, because a clean grid leaves little to tax, and the program adds about 7 points of GDP to public debt by 2050 for little growth. The lite models are not their parents and do not replace them.

The core these upgrades extend is in section 5, which states the mitigation module, rebuilds it and checks it. The instruments they measure are in section 1, the de-risking that sets the cost of capital is in section 3, and the diagnostics that apply the same reproducibility standard to data ministries already hold are in section 7.
